text: Most points at club level are decided in the first three balls. Ten minutes of serves a session pays off fast.
A good short serve would bounce twice on the other side. If it would bounce once, it can be looped.
After contact, keep the bat moving. A follow-through hides which spin you used.
Long serves must be fast and low, aimed at the corners or the elbow. A slow long serve is a free attack.
Serve from the same spot with different spins. It's easier to hide your serve than to hide where you stand.
The reverse pendulum makes the return come out on the other side. Learn it to give your third ball a second option.
The tomahawk works well short to the forehand: the sidespin pulls the return wide.
The backhand serve leaves you square and close, ready for a fast backhand third ball.
Bounce the ball the same number of times before every serve. Routine calms nerves and steadies the toss.
Don't hide the ball with your body or free arm: it's illegal. Hide the spin with the swing instead.
After a short backspin serve, expect a push. After a long serve, expect an attack. Stand ready for the likely ball.
You don't have to attack every third ball. Attack the ones you can, and push or block the rest well.
Build two or three serve patterns you trust, like 'short backspin to the forehand, loop the long push'. Then use them on big points.
There are three great targets: wide forehand, wide backhand, and the playing elbow. Use all three.
Change direction on a ball you have time for, not on a hard one. Down the line is a longer risk.
A ball straight at the hip is awkward for almost everyone. When in doubt, play into the body.
Players love rhythm. Break it: one slow ball after three fast ones is often enough.
Vary length as well as direction. Short-long-short makes people move in and out, which tires them fast.
Against a chopper: loop with spin to the middle, be patient, drop short now and then, and attack only the loose ball.
Against long pimples, your own spin comes back reversed. Heavy topspin returns as backspin: be ready to lift.
Against a blocker, slow spinny loops are better than fast ones: they give no pace to use.
Against a big looper, keep the ball short and low, and block into the body when they open.
Against a penhold player with a strong forehand, play long to the backhand, then switch wide to the forehand.
Against a left-hander, the cross-court diagonals are mirrored. Their forehand covers your forehand cross-court: go down the line more.
In the first few points, test: short, long, fast, slow. Find what they don't like, then keep doing it.
Don't change a winning pattern. Change a losing one, and only one thing at a time.
Use your timeout when the opponent wins three or four points in a row, not only at the end.
At 9–9, play your normal shot with more margin. Big points are not the time for new shots.
A tiny hop as your opponent hits sets your legs to spring either way.
Stay at the same height when you move. Bobbing up and down makes every stroke different.
The first step decides if you get there. Make it quick and small.
Pivot only for balls you can attack. Pivoting for a defensive ball leaves the whole forehand open.
After a cross-over, recover with side steps. Two cross-overs in a row usually means you were too late.
Short ball: in with the playing-side foot. Then push off that same foot to get back out.
Moving in and out is tiring because you stand up between balls. Stay low and it gets easier.
Strong legs fix a lot of 'technique' problems. Lunges and quick feet twice a week make a difference.
Your core links legs to arm. A weak middle leaks power and strains the back.
Do a few slow shoulder rotations with a light band after playing. Healthy shoulders are a long-term investment.
Sleep is training too. Skills settle in overnight; a tired brain learns slowly.
Drink water between drills, not just at the end. Even mild thirst slows your reactions.
Sharp pain means stop. Tiredness is fine; pain is a signal, not a challenge.
Coming back after a break: start with half the volume and build up over two weeks. Tendons need longer than muscles.
Quick feet drills train the nervous system: short, fast and fresh beats long and slow.
After a point, turn away from the table for a moment. It's a physical way to leave the last point behind.
Before a match, choose one thing to focus on. A head full of instructions plays slowly.
Nerves are normal. They mean you care. Breathe out slowly and play your plan.
Think about how you play the next point, not the score. The score takes care of itself.
Stand tall between points even when losing. Body language changes how you feel and how they see you.
Treat a missed easy ball like a missed serve in practice: notice it, let it go, play the next one.
Picture your best serve and third ball before you sleep. Rehearsing in your head helps the real thing.
Learning a new stroke? Make it slow and right first. Speed added to a wrong shape just makes it wrong faster.
Shadow strokes in front of a mirror or a dark window show you what your body really does.
Film yourself from the side once a month. It's the quickest honest coach you have.
Multiball gives you more good repetitions in 5 minutes than a rally gives in 15. Use it for new strokes.
Regular drills build the stroke; random drills build the player. You need both.
Short breaks between sets keep the quality high. Tired repetitions teach tired technique.
Feeding multiball for your partner trains you too: you learn spin by making it.
With a robot, change one setting at a time: spin, speed or placement. Changing all three teaches nothing.
Against a rebound board, aim for a steady rhythm before anything else. The board returns your mistakes too.
Clean your rubbers after every session with water or a cleaner. Dirty rubber loses grip and spin.
Choose control over speed in your equipment until you can loop consistently. Fast rubbers hide technique problems.
At tournaments, warm up your serves before every match, not just your strokes.
Long tournament days: eat small and often. A banana between matches beats a big lunch.
Write one line after each match: what worked, what didn't. Read it before the next one.
